title: A chapter that opens with no Bismillah.
subtitle: A public release from broken agreements
then: This was one of the last surahs revealed, in the ninth year after the Hijrah. The Prophet ﷺ sent Abu Bakr to lead the Hajj, then sent Ali after him to read these verses aloud to the tribes gathered there. {idea}Nothing was hidden. The change was announced to everyone at once.{/idea}
now: You need to end something: a business partnership, a shared flat, a role you can no longer carry. The easy way is to go quiet and let people guess. {idea}Saying it clearly, with notice, is a kindness{/idea} even when the news is hard.
old: If I need out, I can just fade away and let them figure it out.
new: Even an ending can be done honestly, out loud, with fair notice.
try: Think of one thing you have been quietly drifting away from. Tell the person plainly where you stand.

title: Four months of freedom, and no escaping Allah.
subtitle: A grace period before the change took effect
then: The idolaters with open-ended treaties were given {reward}four months to travel the land safely{/reward} and decide what to do. The proclamation was read on the day of Arafah. The same breath reminded them that {trap}no one can escape Allah{/trap}.
now: The doctor says: you have a few months to change your diet before this becomes serious. The manager says: here is time to improve. {idea}A deadline with mercy built in{/idea} is a gift, if you use it to turn rather than to wait it out.
old: A long deadline means I can relax for now.
new: A grace period is mercy, given so I can change before it ends.
try: Pick one warning you have been given lately. Take the first small step on it today.

title: Announced on the biggest day, with repentance still offered.
subtitle: A warning that ends on an invitation
then: On the day of Sacrifice, when the greatest number of pilgrims gathered at Mina, Ali and others called out the announcement. Even in this stern moment, the verse says to the listeners: {reward}if you repent, that is better for you.{/reward}
now: Someone tells you a hard truth about yourself, maybe in front of others. It stings. But listen to the end of the sentence: {idea}there is almost always a way back offered{/idea}. The warning is there so you take it.
old: When I am warned, it means I have already been written off.
new: Allah's warnings come with the door of repentance held open.
try: Make a short, honest tawbah tonight for one specific thing. Name it to Allah.

title: Those who kept their word kept their treaty.
subtitle: Honoring agreements to the last day
then: Some tribes had treaties with a fixed end date and had never broken them or helped anyone against the Muslims. For them, {idea}the treaty stood until its last day{/idea}. Ibn Kathir explains the muttaqin here as those who keep their promises.
now: You agreed to a contract, a rent, a shift swap, a favor for a friend. Then things changed and a better deal appeared. {reward}Allah loves the one who finishes the term anyway{/reward}, even when no one would blame you for wriggling out.
old: When circumstances change, my old promises bend with them.
new: A promise to someone who kept faith with me runs until its end.
try: Find one commitment you are tempted to drop early. Finish it as agreed.

title: Even the sternest verse ends with forgiveness and mercy.
subtitle: After the sacred months, the way back stays open
then: This verse spoke to a specific moment: when the four-month grace period ended, the state of war with those idolaters of Arabia would resume, though Ibn Kathir notes it excludes the Sacred Area. Yet it closes with {reward}if they repent, pray and give zakah, let them go their way{/reward}, and {idea}Allah is Forgiving, Merciful.{/idea}
now: Think of a time you were sure someone had gone too far for any second chance. Maybe the someone was you. {idea}This verse does not end on the hard part.{/idea} It ends on a way back and on Allah's mercy, and that ending is for you too.
old: Once things get this serious, there is no way back.
new: Even at the hardest point, Allah leaves the path of return open.
try: Pray one prayer today with the intention of coming back to Allah, whatever you carry.

title: Protect him, let him listen, then walk him home safely.
subtitle: Safe passage for anyone who asks

row.title: he does not know yet
sub: give him a chance to hear

then: In the middle of verses about war, any idolater who asked for protection was to be given it, allowed to {idea}hear the Quran{/idea}, and then {reward}escorted to safety{/reward}. Ibn Kathir mentions the envoys of Quraysh at Hudaybiyyah, who went home amazed at what they had seen.
now: Someone who disagrees with you sharply asks a sincere question. You could score a point or shut them out. {idea}The verse says: make them safe, let them hear, see them off well.{/idea} They may not know what you know.
old: People on the other side of an argument do not deserve my patience.
new: Someone asking to understand deserves safety and a fair hearing.
try: Next time someone asks you a sincere question about your faith, answer gently and thank them.

title: As long as they stay straight with you, stay straight.
subtitle: Faithfulness answers faithfulness

row.title: never be the one who breaks

then: The treaty of Hudaybiyyah, made near the Sacred Mosque, was kept by the Muslims from the sixth year {idea}until Quraysh themselves broke it{/idea} by helping Banu Bakr attack Khuza'ah. Ibn Kathir notes that some who fled later, like Ikrimah, were given safety and {reward}became excellent believers.{/reward}
now: A colleague, a neighbor, an in-law you do not get along with. As long as they keep their side, {idea}keep yours fully{/idea}, no small digs, no quiet sabotage. Let it never be you who broke the peace.
old: I keep my word only with people I like.
new: If they stay straight with me, I stay straight with them, liked or not.
try: With one difficult person, do your part of the arrangement perfectly this week.

title: Sweet words from the mouth, refusal in the heart.
subtitle: When the tongue and the heart disagree

row.title: hearts refuse
sub: no regard for kinship or pact

then: The verse explains why some of those treaties could not last: if those parties gained the upper hand, {trap}they would respect neither kinship (ill) nor pledge (dhimmah){/trap}, as Ibn Abbas defined the words. {trap}They pleased with their mouths while their hearts refused.{/trap}
now: "Sure, I'll be there." "No problem, happy to help." Said with a smile, while inside you have already decided not to. Before judging others with this verse, {idea}check how often your own yes is only in the mouth.{/idea}
old: Saying yes to keep the peace is harmless, even if I don't mean it.
new: A yes the heart refuses is a small betrayal. Let my words match me.
try: Today, say no kindly to one thing you would have said a fake yes to.

title: They sold Allah's signs for a small price.
subtitle: Trading the truth for a little gain
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the idolaters {trap}gave up following Allah's signs for the lower affairs of this life{/trap} and then tried to keep the believers from the truth as well. Losing guidance yourself and blocking others from it were joined.
now: The promotion that needs a small lie. Skipping prayer for one more hour of overtime. Laughing along when religion is mocked, to stay in the group. {trap}Every price paid for leaving the truth is small{/trap}, compared to what you give away.
old: It is just this once, and what I get is worth it.
new: Anything I take in exchange for Allah's guidance is a small price.
try: Notice one small compromise you make for convenience. Skip it once today.

title: No regard for kinship, no regard for a pledge.
subtitle: The ones who overstep every bond
then: The previous verse said they would not honor ties if they gained power over the Muslims. This verse widens it: {trap}toward any believer at all{/trap}, they respected neither kinship nor covenant. It is they, the verse says, who {trap}were the aggressors.{/trap}
now: When you are angry with a cousin or a former friend, it is tempting to forget everything you owe them. The shared childhood, the favor they did, the promise you made. {idea}Hold on to the ties even when you are hurt.{/idea} That is the opposite of what this verse describes.
old: Once someone wrongs me, I owe them nothing anymore.
new: Family ties and promises still count, even when I am angry.
try: Send one kind message to a relative you have been cold toward.

title: Yesterday's opponents can become today's brothers.
subtitle: Repentance turns enemies into family
then: Right after describing those who broke every bond, the verse opens the widest door: {reward}if they repent, pray and give zakah, they are your brothers in religion.{/reward} Ibn Kathir mentions men of Makkah who once fought and later became excellent believers.
now: Someone who hurt you, or mocked your faith, turns around and changes. They show up at the masjid, or apologize. {idea}The verse asks you to call them brother, not to keep a file on them.{/idea}
old: People who once opposed me will always be suspect.
new: When someone truly turns back to Allah, they become my family.
try: Greet warmly someone whose past you know. Let it stay in the past.

title: When an oath means nothing to the one who swore it.
subtitle: Leaders who broke their word
then: This addressed the idolaters of Quraysh who had sworn treaties and then broke them while attacking the faith. Qatadah named leaders of Makkah's opposition such as Abu Jahl and Umayyah bin Khalaf. The stated goal: {idea}that they might stop.{/idea}
now: "I swear I'll pay you back." "Wallahi I'll be there." How easily the oath comes out, and how easily it is forgotten. The verse describes people for whom {trap}oaths meant nothing.{/trap} {idea}Make sure your own wallahi still weighs something.{/idea}
old: Swearing by Allah is just a way to make people believe me.
new: An oath by Allah is heavy. If I say it, I keep it.
try: Stop using wallahi casually for one day. Save it for what you truly mean.

title: Do you fear them? Allah has more right to be feared.
subtitle: Which fear runs your decisions
then: The believers were reminded that these opponents had {trap}broken their oaths, plotted to drive the Prophet ﷺ out of Makkah, and attacked first{/trap}, which Ibn Kathir links to Badr. Some still hesitated. The question cut through it: {idea}do you fear them? Allah has more right to be feared.{/idea}
now: You know the right thing to say in the meeting, but you fear the boss. You know you should stop the gossip, but you fear the group. {idea}Ask yourself whose reaction you are really afraid of.{/idea} Then weigh it against Allah's.
old: I stay quiet because of what people might do to me.
new: People's reactions are small next to what Allah sees and decides.
try: Do one right thing today that you have been avoiding out of fear of someone's reaction.

title: Allah could act alone, yet chose to act through them.
subtitle: Being the hands through which Allah helps

row.title: Allah
sub: able to act by a word

row.title: I need to take part
sub: it is my test and honor

then: Ibn Kathir notes that Allah could destroy the enemies by a single command, yet asked the believers to strive, and promised {reward}victory and the healing of believing hearts{/reward}. Some early scholars said the wounded hearts were those of Khuza'ah, the allies attacked while under treaty.
now: A neighbor needs help moving. A friend is grieving. You think: Allah will take care of them. {idea}Often He takes care of them through you{/idea}, and the healing in their chest begins with your knock on the door.
old: If Allah wants something done, it will happen without me.
new: Allah lets me be part of how His help arrives. That is an honor.
try: Be the answer to someone's prayer today: one call, one errand, one meal.

title: Anger leaves the heart, and repentance stays possible.
subtitle: Relief for the wronged, a door for the wrongdoer
then: The believers had carried {trap}anger at broken treaties and attacks{/trap} for years. Allah promised to remove that fury from their hearts. Then, in the same verse, a reminder that {idea}Allah turns in mercy to whom He wills{/idea}, even among those they had been fighting.
now: You have been wronged, and the anger sits in your chest every time you see their name on your phone. {reward}Ask Allah to take the fury out of you.{/reward} And leave room for the thought that they might change. That is His business, not yours.
old: My anger will only go when they get what they deserve.
new: Allah can lift my anger, and He can still guide the one I am angry at.
try: Make dua today for your anger to be removed, and for the one who wronged you to be guided.

title: Did you think you would be left without a test?
subtitle: Tests show who is sincere
then: Ibn Kathir explains that one wisdom behind these hard commands was {idea}to test the believers{/idea}, making clear who was sincere and who kept secret allies apart from Allah, His Messenger ﷺ and the believers. He ties it to {idea}"Do people think they will be left because they say we believe?"{/idea}
now: Faith is easy on a calm Friday. Then comes the job loss, the diagnosis, the moment when standing with the right people costs you. {idea}That is where your faith becomes visible, first to you.{/idea}
old: If my faith were real, life would not keep testing it.
new: The test is how sincere faith shows itself, even to me.
try: Name one current difficulty. Ask Allah to help you pass it well, not just escape it.

title: Maintaining a mosque does not replace believing in its Lord.
subtitle: Service without faith at its root
then: The Sacred Mosque was built by Ibrahim for the worship of Allah alone. Yet the idolaters of Makkah held its keys and upkeep {trap}while openly associating partners with Allah{/trap}. The verse says such service, cut off from faith, {trap}becomes worthless.{/trap}
now: You run the masjid's fundraiser, sit on the committee, post the Ramadan schedule. All good. {idea}But ask what is underneath it{/idea}: Allah, or the role, the respect, the title.
old: My service to the community proves my faith.
new: Service counts when it grows from real faith in Allah alone.
try: Before your next act of service, pause and renew your intention for Allah alone.

title: Who truly keeps a mosque alive.
subtitle: The four marks of a real maintainer
then: After saying who cannot rightly maintain the mosques, the verse names who can: {idea}those who believe, pray, give zakah and fear none but Allah.{/idea} Companions said the masjids are the houses of Allah on earth, and {reward}He is generous to those who visit Him there.{/reward}
now: A beautiful masjid with three people at Fajr. A small rented room packed at Isha. {idea}A mosque is kept alive by the people who show up and pray{/idea}, and you can be one of them this week.
old: Keeping up the mosque is the job of the board and the imam.
new: I maintain the mosque every time I come to it to pray.
try: Pray one prayer in the masjid this week that you normally pray at home.

title: Water for pilgrims is not the same as faith.
subtitle: Prestige deeds versus the deeds of the heart
then: Ibn Abbas said the people of Makkah used to boast that {trap}giving water to pilgrims and caring for the Sacred Mosque was better than faith{/trap}. Another report says al-Abbas, captured at Badr, made this argument. A report from An-Nu'man bin Bashir also describes Muslims debating which deed is best near the minbar.
now: You sponsor an orphan, organize the charity run, are known as the generous one. Then someone asks about your prayer, and you point to the charity. {idea}Good deeds are not a trade for the heart's turning to Allah.{/idea}
old: My visible good works make up for what is missing inside.
new: Faith in Allah comes first. Nothing visible stands in for it.
try: Look at one good thing you are known for. Ask whether you do it for Allah or for the name.

title: Believed, left home, gave wealth and self: higher in rank.
subtitle: What real sacrifice looks like
then: In contrast to those who boasted of keeping the Sacred Mosque, this verse describes the early believers who {idea}believed, left their homes, and gave their wealth and their lives{/idea} for Allah. They are {reward}higher in rank with Allah, and they are the successful.{/reward}
now: Status is easy to collect: titles, followers, a good family name. Sacrifice is quieter. Turning down the job that would have cost your prayers. Moving for your family's deen. {reward}That is what raises you with Allah.{/reward}
old: My rank comes from my position and reputation.
new: My rank with Allah comes from what I am willing to give for Him.
try: Give up one comfort today for Allah's sake, quietly, and tell no one.

title: Their Lord sends them good news of mercy and pleasure.
subtitle: The three gifts promised
then: Those who had left Makkah lost homes, families and trade. The verse says {reward}their own Lord gives them the good news{/reward}: mercy from Him, His pleasure, and gardens of lasting delight. What they gave up was replaced from Him directly.
now: You did something hard for Allah's sake and nobody noticed. No thank you, no post, no credit. {reward}The good news is coming from a higher place than the group chat.{/reward}
old: If no one appreciates what I gave up, it was wasted.
new: Allah Himself has promised mercy and His pleasure for what I gave for Him.
try: Recall one sacrifice nobody saw. Thank Allah that He saw it.

title: Forever there, and with Allah is a great reward.
subtitle: A reward that does not end

row.title: it is too much to give

then: The promise to those early believers closes with two words of weight: {reward}forever{/reward}, and {reward}a great reward with Allah{/reward}. Whatever they had lost in a few years of exile and struggle was set against something without end.
now: The night shift so your kids can study. The year of caring for a sick parent. Holding back your anger again and again. It feels endless. {idea}Measured against forever, it is short.{/idea}
old: This sacrifice is costing me too much.
new: Any sacrifice here is short next to a reward that never ends.
try: When something hard comes up today, whisper: with Allah is a great reward.

title: Love your family, but do not let them pull you from faith.
subtitle: When closeness becomes a pull away from Allah
then: In those years, families in Arabia were split: a son believing, a father fighting him. The believers were told not to take as {trap}allies and confidants{/trap} relatives who had chosen disbelief over faith and stood against it. Ibn Kathir links it to {idea}"You will not find a people who believe in Allah... loving those who oppose Allah."{/idea}
now: Your family wants you to skip Jumuah for the reunion, or mocks your hijab, or pushes you toward a deal you know is wrong. You can stay kind and present. {idea}What you cannot do is let their pull decide your faith for you.{/idea}
old: Keeping my family happy comes before everything.
new: I can honor my family and still refuse to let them pull me from Allah.
try: Next time family pressure clashes with your faith, answer with warmth and a clear no.

title: Eight loves on one side, Allah on the other.
subtitle: A checklist of what holds your heart
then: As the believers were called to give and strive, this verse listed {reward}everything a person naturally loves{/reward} and asked which was dearer. Ibn Kathir adds the moment Umar said the Prophet ﷺ was dearer to him than all but himself, and was told faith means {idea}more than yourself too{/idea}. Then Umar said: now you are.
now: Read the list slowly: your parents, your kids, your partner, your savings, your business, your flat you finally decorated. {idea}None is wrong to love.{/idea} The test is the moment one of them asks you to put Allah second. Which one would win?
old: I love Allah most, I just never get asked to prove it.
new: When my loves clash with Allah, the one I choose shows what is first.
try: Read the list in the verse and honestly mark which item would most easily pull you away.

title: Your large numbers pleased you, and gave you nothing.
subtitle: The lesson of Hunayn
then: In the eighth year, just after Makkah, a Muslim army of about twelve thousand marched to Hunayn. {trap}They were pleased with their numbers.{/trap} Hawazin ambushed them in the valley and most fled. {idea}The Prophet ﷺ stayed firm{/idea}, calling out: I am the Prophet, no lie.
now: A full team, a big budget, a strong CV, a big family behind you. You walk in sure it cannot go wrong, and it does. {idea}Prepare well, but put your trust in Allah, not in the size of what you have.{/idea}
old: With all this behind me, I cannot fail.
new: No amount of people or resources replaces relying on Allah.
try: Before your next big task, say a short dua asking Allah for success instead of counting your advantages.

title: Then came calm from Allah, and help no one saw.
subtitle: Sakinah after panic
then: Al-Abbas called out to the companions of the Pledge under the Tree, and the fleeing Muslims answered: here we are. They returned to the Prophet ﷺ. Allah then {reward}sent down His calm on His Messenger and the believers{/reward}, and {reward}soldiers they did not see.{/reward}
now: The test results come back bad. The business collapses. Your mind races and you want to run. {idea}Turn back toward Allah, even after a first panic.{/idea} Calm is something He sends down; ask for it.
old: Once I have panicked and failed, it is too late.
new: Even after I run, I can turn back, and Allah can send calm.
try: In your next anxious moment, stop and ask Allah for sakinah by name.

title: After the battle, the door of repentance stayed open.
subtitle: Yesterday's opponent, forgiven

row.title: Allah may still turn to them

then: Right after describing the defeat of those who fought at Hunayn, the verse adds: {reward}after that, Allah turns in mercy to whom He wills.{/reward} The ones who had just been fighting the believers were not shut out from forgiveness.
now: You lost the argument badly, or you were the one in the wrong. The defeat feels like the end of the story. {idea}It does not have to be.{/idea} After the loss comes the chance to turn back to Allah.
old: After what I did, there is no coming back.
new: Even after a failure or defeat, Allah's forgiveness is still on offer.
try: Think of a recent failure. Turn it into one sincere istighfar today.

title: Afraid of losing income? Allah will enrich you.
subtitle: When doing right threatens your livelihood
then: In the ninth year, it was ruled that after that season the idolaters would no longer come to the Sacred Mosque. Ibn Ishaq reports the people's fear: {trap}our markets will close and our earnings will vanish.{/trap} The reply: {reward}Allah will enrich you from His bounty, if He wills.{/reward}
now: Your biggest client wants you to cut a corner. Refusing could cost you the account, the rent, the school fees. {reward}The verse speaks straight to that fear{/reward}: your provision was never in that one door.
old: If I do the right thing, I will lose my income.
new: My provision comes from Allah, who has more doors than I can see.
try: Name one money fear that keeps you from doing right. Say: Allah will enrich me from His bounty.

title: The call that led to Tabuk, in drought and heat.
subtitle: The setting of the hard march north
then: Ibn Kathir places this verse in the ninth year, when the command came to fight the People of the Book and the Prophet ﷺ prepared to march against the Romans. {trap}It was a year of drought and intense heat.{/trap} About thirty thousand marched to Tabuk, camped about twenty days, and returned. {trap}Some, including hypocrites, stayed behind.{/trap}
now: The hard call never comes in an easy season. The parent needs care during your busiest year. The fast comes in the longest days. {idea}This part of the surah is about who answers when it costs something{/idea}, and you are asked that question in your own life.
old: I will answer Allah's call once things get easier.
new: The call that matters often comes in the hardest season. That is the test.
try: Do one act of obedience today that you have been postponing until life is less busy.

title: Words from the mouth, with no proof behind them.
subtitle: Saying things about Allah without knowledge
then: The verse addresses claims made at the time that Allah had a son, {trap}"a saying from their mouths"{/trap}, Ibn Kathir explains, with no proof, {trap}imitating what earlier peoples had said.{/trap} The surah answers it with pure tawhid: Allah alone, without partner or child.
now: You repeat something about Allah you heard on a video or from an uncle: "Allah will never forgive that," "this dua guarantees anything." Is it from Allah, or just from mouths? {idea}Check what you say about Allah before you say it.{/idea}
old: If many people say it about Allah, it must be right.
new: What I say about Allah needs to come from Him, not from repetition.
try: Pick one belief you hold about Allah. Look up its source in the Quran or a sound hadith.

title: Obeying people over Allah is a form of worship.
subtitle: The question Adi bin Hatim asked
then: Adi bin Hatim, chief of Tayy, came to Madinah and heard this verse. He said: they did not worship their scholars. The Prophet ﷺ replied that {trap}they made lawful what was forbidden and forbade what was lawful, and people followed{/trap}. {idea}That obedience was the worship.{/idea} Adi accepted Islam that day.
now: Your boss, your favorite influencer, your friend group, even a popular preacher. When one of them says something Allah made clear is fine is wrong, or the reverse, and you go along without thinking, {idea}ask whose word you are really following.{/idea}
old: As long as I do not bow to anyone, I am worshipping only Allah.
new: Whoever I obey over Allah in what is lawful and unlawful, I have raised up.
try: Think of one thing you do only because someone you admire says so. Check what Allah says about it.

title: Blowing at the sun to put it out.
subtitle: Allah's light will be completed

row.title: Allah perfects it
sub: my job is to walk in it

then: Ibn Kathir says those who tried to put out the guidance with {trap}argument and lies{/trap} are like {trap}someone blowing at the sun or the moon to extinguish it.{/trap} He also notes kafir comes from covering, like night covering things or a farmer covering seed.
now: You read a viral thread mocking Islam and feel your stomach drop, as if the truth itself is in danger. {reward}It is not.{/reward} Allah will complete His light. {idea}Your part is to keep it lit in your own home and heart.{/idea}
old: Every attack on the faith makes me afraid it will fade.
new: Allah has promised to complete His light. I only need to walk in it.
try: Instead of scrolling one more argument online, read one page of Quran today.

title: Sent with guidance and the religion of truth.
subtitle: What the Messenger ﷺ brought
then: Ibn Kathir explains guidance as {idea}the true reports and beneficial faith{/idea} the Prophet ﷺ brought, and the religion of truth as {idea}the righteous deeds that benefit in this life and the next.{/idea} Tamim Ad-Dari, once a Christian, said he saw goodness and honor come to those of his people who accepted it.
now: You may never shape what happens on a world stage. But there is a small territory you do govern: your tongue, your phone, your mornings. {idea}Let the guidance prevail there first.{/idea}
old: Islam's success is about what happens far away from me.
new: The guidance prevails first in the life I actually run.
try: Choose one habit today and bring it in line with what the Prophet ﷺ taught.

title: Religion used as income, and wealth locked away.
subtitle: Three kinds of leaders, and how they go wrong
then: The verse describes religious figures at the time who {trap}used their position to take people's wealth unjustly{/trap} and turned them from Allah's way, and those who hoarded gold and silver without spending in His cause. Sufyan bin Uyaynah drew the lesson inward: {idea}when our own scholars and worshippers go wrong, they become like them.{/idea}
now: You lead a halaqa, run a charity page, or are the one at work people ask about deen. {trap}It is easy to let a little status or money ride on it.{/trap} And the savings sitting untouched while a relative struggles: {idea}whose is it, really?{/idea}
old: This warning is about corrupt people somewhere else.
new: Anyone with knowledge, piety or money can misuse it, including me.
try: Check that the zakah or sadaqah you owe on your savings has gone where it should.

title: What you held onto becomes what you carry.
subtitle: The hoarded wealth returns on the Day
then: The verse describes the Day when that hoarded gold and silver {trap}is brought back against its owners{/trap}, with the words: {trap}this is what you stored up for yourselves.{/trap} Ibn Kathir notes a saying: whoever prefers a thing over obeying Allah is punished by that very thing.
now: The extra account you never mention, the cash you keep "just in case" while your sister cannot pay rent. {idea}What you clutch hardest can become the heaviest thing you bring.{/idea} Spending some of it now is the way out.
old: The more I keep, the safer I am.
new: Wealth I never use for Allah can turn from safety into burden.
try: Give something today from money you have been holding onto for no clear reason.

title: Twelve months, four sacred: do not wrong yourselves in them.
subtitle: Some times carry more weight
then: In his Farewell Hajj the Prophet ﷺ said time had come round to its original form: {idea}twelve months, four of them sacred{/idea}, three in a row and Rajab alone. Qatadah said wrongdoing is always wrong, but {trap}heavier in the sacred months{/trap}, and Allah has chosen some times above others.
now: Muharram comes, or Dhul-Hijjah, and your phone calendar treats it like any other month. {idea}Mark it.{/idea} Hold your tongue more, give a little more, avoid the argument. These months are a season Allah chose.
old: Every month is the same as any other.
new: Allah gave some months extra weight. I can live them with extra care.
try: Put the four sacred months in your phone calendar, with one goal for each.

title: Moving the sacred month to fit their plans.
subtitle: Keeping the count, breaking the meaning
then: Before Islam, some Arabs found three sacred months in a row too long to go without raiding. A man of Kinanah would announce at Hajj that {trap}Muharram was moved to Safar{/trap} that year. They kept the count at four, but {trap}made lawful what Allah had made sacred{/trap}, and their evil deeds were made to seem fine to them.
now: "I'll fast a different day, this week is busy." "I'll pray all of them together at night." Small shuffles that keep the look of obedience. {idea}Notice when you rearrange Allah's limits to fit your schedule.{/idea}
old: As long as the total adds up, the timing does not matter.
new: Bending Allah's rules to fit my plans is not keeping them.
try: Pray the next prayer on time, even if it means moving something else.

title: Clinging heavily to the ground when called to rise.
subtitle: Shade and ripe fruit versus the call
then: The call to march to Tabuk came {trap}when fruit was ripe, shade was tempting and the heat was intense.{/trap} Some believers felt heavy and stayed. The Prophet ﷺ compared this world to the next as {idea}a finger dipped in the sea: see what it brings back.{/idea}
now: The alarm for Fajr on a cold morning. The call to visit a sick friend on your one free evening. {trap}You feel that heaviness pulling you down into the sofa.{/trap} {idea}Look at your finger, then at the sea.{/idea}
old: Comfort now is worth more than something I cannot see.
new: This world next to the next is a drop on my finger next to the ocean.
try: The next time you feel that heaviness before a good deed, get up within ten seconds.

title: Allah does not need you. You need to be part of it.
subtitle: Replaceable, and still invited
then: Those hanging back from Tabuk were warned of a painful punishment, and that {idea}Allah would replace them with another people{/idea} who would support His Prophet ﷺ. {idea}You will not harm Him at all.{/idea} Ibn Kathir cites a similar verse: they will not be like you.
now: You drop out of the masjid volunteer team, the family support rota, the Quran circle. It carries on fine without you. {trap}The loss is yours, not theirs.{/trap} The good work was always going to be done.
old: If I step back, things will fall apart without me.
new: Allah's work goes on regardless. The honor of being part of it is what I lose.
try: Rejoin one good effort you quietly dropped out of.

title: Do not grieve. Allah is with us.
subtitle: Two in a cave, and Allah the third

row.title: two men
sub: the Prophet ﷺ and Abu Bakr

key.label: How many were in the cave

row.title: Allah with them
sub: what do you think of two?

then: When Makkah drove him out, the Prophet ﷺ hid with Abu Bakr in the cave of Thawr for three days. Abu Bakr whispered that if one of the pursuers looked at his feet, he would see them. The Prophet ﷺ said: {reward}what do you think of two when Allah is their third?{/reward} {idea}Do not grieve, Allah is with us.{/idea}
now: The hospital corridor at 3am. The night before the court date. The message you are dreading to open. {reward}You are not two, or one. Allah is with you.{/reward} Say the words the Prophet ﷺ said in that cave.
old: When I am cornered, I am on my own.
new: In the tightest place, Allah is with me, and that changes everything.
try: In your next frightening moment, say quietly: la tahzan, inna Allaha ma'ana.

title: Go forth, light or heavy.
subtitle: Answering the call in any condition

row.title: light or heavy
sub: the state you are in now

then: This call came for Tabuk, asking for everyone to march. The elderly Abu Talhah, reading it years later, told his sons: {idea}Allah has called us old or young{/idea}, and set out once more. Ibn Kathir also notes the later verse that lifted blame from {reward}the weak, the ill and those with nothing to spend.{/reward}
now: You are waiting to feel motivated before you start memorizing, or to have more money before you give, or less stress before you help. {idea}Go as you are, light or heavy.{/idea} The mood follows the step.
old: I will do good when I am in the right state for it.
new: I go in whatever state I am in. That is what the call asks.
try: Start one good deed today in the mood you are in, without waiting to feel ready.

title: If it were quick and easy, they would have come.
subtitle: Excuses sworn by Allah
then: Ibn Kathir says this addressed the hypocrites who stayed behind from Tabuk. {trap}Had it been nearby gain and a short journey, they would have come.{/trap} But the road to Syria was long. On his return they would swear: {trap}if we could, we would have gone.{/trap} Allah knew they were lying.
now: The charity event is two hours away, so you suddenly have a headache. The study circle is on a rainy night, so you are "swamped." {idea}Be honest with yourself about the difference between cannot and will not.{/idea}
old: I would have helped, I just could not this time.
new: Many of my can'ts are won'ts. Allah knows which is which.
try: The next time you give an excuse, ask yourself honestly if it would stand if the task were easy.

title: Allah pardoned him before He asked him why.
subtitle: The gentlest correction in the Quran
then: When the hypocrites asked to stay home, the Prophet ﷺ gave them permission. This verse gently questioned it: had he waited, the truthful and the liars would have been clear. Awn said: {reward}have you heard a softer rebuke, beginning with forgiveness before blame?{/reward}
now: Your child broke something. Your colleague made an error in the report. Before the "why did you...", {reward}start with warmth{/reward}: "It's alright, may Allah make it easy." {idea}Then make your point.{/idea}
old: To correct someone, I have to start with what they did wrong.
new: Even Allah's correction began with pardon. Mine can start with kindness.
try: The next time you need to correct someone today, open with a kind word first.

title: Those who believe do not look for the way out.
subtitle: Faith runs toward the hard thing
then: Ibn Kathir explains that believers in Allah and the Last Day {idea}did not ask leave to stay behind{/idea} from striving with their wealth and lives, {idea}because they saw it as worship{/idea}. When the call came, they hurried to it. Allah knows those who are mindful of Him.
now: A relative needs a carer this month. The masjid needs someone to clean on Saturday. Your first thought shows a lot: {trap}"who else can do it?"{/trap} or {idea}"when do they need me?"{/idea}
old: My first move with a hard task is to see if I can get out of it.
new: Faith makes my first question how I can help, not how I can escape.
try: Say yes today to one request you would normally try to dodge.

title: One step forward, one step back.
subtitle: What doubt does to a person
then: Those asking to stay home from Tabuk without a real excuse were, the verse says, people whose {trap}hearts were in doubt.{/trap} Ibn Kathir describes them as {trap}taking one step forward and one step back{/trap}, never firm in anything, belonging neither to one side nor the other.
now: You keep half-committing: to the prayer routine, the hijab, the Quran plan, leaving the bad habit. In on Monday, out by Thursday. {idea}Ask what doubt is underneath{/idea}, and bring that doubt to Allah instead of living inside it.
old: I am not doubting, I am just keeping my options open.
new: Constant wavering often hides a doubt I need to face honestly.
try: Write down one doubt you carry about your faith. Look for a real answer this week.

title: If they meant to go, they would have packed.
subtitle: Intention shows up as preparation
then: Those who stayed behind claimed they would have gone. The verse answers simply: {idea}had they meant to go, they would have prepared something.{/idea} Instead, Allah held them back, and it was said: {trap}sit with those who sit.{/trap}
now: "I really want to do Hajj." No savings account for it. "I want to learn Arabic." No book, no app, no teacher. {idea}What you truly intend leaves traces in your week.{/idea}
old: I mean to do it. That counts for something.
new: Real intention shows in preparation, even a small first step.
try: Pick one good goal you keep talking about. Do one concrete thing to prepare for it today.

title: Had they come, they would have added only confusion.
subtitle: Some people add disorder, and some will listen
then: Ibn Ishaq names Abdullah bin Ubayy and Al-Jadd bin Qays among those who asked to stay. Had they gone, the verse says, {trap}they would have spread false stories and discord in the ranks{/trap}, and {trap}some among the believers would have listened to them{/trap}, respecting their status.
now: There is a voice in your family WhatsApp, your office, your masjid committee that always stirs things up. {idea}This verse is also about the listeners.{/idea} You do not have to be the one who forwards it.
old: I am just listening, I am not the one stirring things.
new: Eagerly listening to troublemakers is how their discord spreads.
try: The next time someone shares divisive gossip, do not reply and do not forward it.

title: They plotted long before, and the truth came anyway.
subtitle: Schemes that could not stop what Allah willed
then: Ibn Kathir explains that from the early days in Madinah, the hypocrites had {trap}plotted and turned matters upside down.{/trap} After Badr, Abdullah bin Ubayy and his circle said this matter has prevailed and accepted Islam outwardly. {reward}Yet the truth came and Allah's command became clear{/reward}, though they disliked it.
now: Someone at work has been undermining you for months, twisting what you say. It is exhausting. {reward}Do your work honestly and leave the outcome to Allah.{/reward} Schemes look powerful up close.
old: If people plot against me, they will win.
new: Plots can delay and hurt, but they do not override what Allah decrees.
try: Make a short dua about someone working against you, then do your next task well and let it go.

title: Excuse me so I am not tested, and that was the test.
subtitle: A pious-sounding excuse
then: Al-Jadd bin Qays told the Prophet ﷺ: let me stay, {trap}do not put me into temptation{/trap}, for if I see the Roman women I will not be patient. The Prophet ﷺ turned away and gave him leave. Ibn Kathir explains the verse: {trap}staying behind was itself the greater fitnah{/trap}, worse than the one he claimed to fear.
now: "I don't go to the masjid, the people there are judgmental." "I don't give because charities might misuse it." {idea}A spiritual-sounding excuse can be the very trap.{/idea} Look at what the excuse is protecting.
old: I avoid this good deed to protect my faith.
new: Sometimes my pious excuse is the trial I am failing.
try: Look at one religious-sounding reason you give for skipping something good. Test whether it is real.

title: Your good news hurt them, your hardship pleased them.
subtitle: Watch what you feel at others' news
then: The hypocrites were {trap}upset when the Prophet ﷺ and his companions had victory{/trap}, and when hardship came they said, {trap}we took our precautions by staying out of it{/trap}, and turned away pleased. Ibn Kathir calls it the depth of their enmity.
now: Your cousin's business takes off and something sour rises in you. A colleague fails and you feel a tiny glow of "told you so." {idea}Catch that feeling.{/idea} It is the exact reaction this verse describes.
old: A little satisfaction when others fail is only human.
new: Being glad at a believer's hardship is a sign to heal my heart.
try: Congratulate, sincerely, someone whose success you felt a pang about.

title: Nothing reaches us except what Allah has written.
subtitle: The answer to I told you so
then: To those who mocked the believers' hardships and praised their own caution, the Prophet ﷺ was told to say: {idea}nothing will strike us except what Allah has decreed for us. He is our protector.{/idea} And upon Allah let the believers rely.
now: "I told you not to quit that job." "You should never have moved." When things go wrong after a sincere choice, the I-told-you-sos pile up. {reward}What reached you was written, and He is your Mawla.{/reward}
old: If something bad happened, I must have chosen wrong.
new: Only what Allah wrote reaches me, and He is my protector in it.
try: Say this verse once today about something that went wrong: lan yusibana illa ma kataballahu lana.

title: Either way, the believer gets one of two good things.
subtitle: No losing outcome for one who strives for Allah
then: The hypocrites sat waiting for misfortune to fall on the believers. The reply: {reward}what are you waiting for except one of two best things?{/reward} Ibn Abbas and others said: {reward}victory or martyrdom.{/reward} Both were good for the believer.
now: You give your sincere best to something: an exam, a hard conversation, caring for a parent. Either it works, or you are rewarded for the striving. {reward}With Allah, sincere effort never ends in a total loss.{/reward}
old: If it does not work out, all my effort was wasted.
new: Sincere striving for Allah wins either way, in result or in reward.
try: Pick one effort you fear might fail. Renew your intention for Allah and keep going.

title: Spending without faith behind it is not accepted.
subtitle: Money is not the whole of a gift
then: The hypocrites were told: {trap}spend willingly or unwillingly, it will not be accepted from you.{/trap} Ibn Kathir notes that {idea}Allah is Good and accepts only what is good{/idea}, from people of taqwa.
now: You transfer a donation to make the guilt go away, or so your name appears on the list. {idea}Allah looks for what is behind the transfer.{/idea} A small amount given with faith outweighs a large one given to be seen.
old: As long as I give a lot, the reason does not matter.
new: Allah accepts what is given with faith, not just the size of it.
try: Give a small amount today, secretly, purely for Allah.

title: Coming to prayer lazily, giving reluctantly.
subtitle: Three signs worth checking in yourself

row.title: no real faith
sub: in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ

then: The verse explains why their spending was refused: {trap}they disbelieved, came to prayer only lazily, and spent only unwillingly.{/trap} Ibn Kathir notes they had {trap}neither good intention nor eagerness{/trap} for acts of faith.
now: Everyone has days of dragging to prayer and sighing at the charity box. {idea}The danger is when it becomes your settled way.{/idea} Use the verse as a mirror, not a weapon. How do you come to salah most days?
old: As long as I pray and give, how I feel about it is irrelevant.
new: Laziness in prayer and reluctance in giving are signs to treat early.
try: For your next prayer, make wudu slowly and arrive a few minutes early.

title: Do not be dazzled by their money and their children.
subtitle: What looks like blessing can be a burden
then: The Prophet ﷺ was told not to be impressed by the hypocrites' wealth and sons. Ibn Kathir links it to {idea}"do not strain your eyes toward the splendor We gave them to test them."{/idea} He warns of {trap}being led on gradually by what one has{/trap}, and seeks refuge from such an end.
now: Scrolling through someone's holiday photos, new car, picture-perfect family, and feeling your own life shrink. {idea}What you see is not the whole story, and it is not the measure of anyone's standing with Allah.{/idea} Including yours.
old: People with more money and a big family must be blessed by Allah.
new: Wealth and children can be a test. What matters is where they lead.
try: Unfollow or mute one account that makes you envious, for a week.

title: Swearing they belong, out of fear, not love.
subtitle: Belonging that is only for safety
then: The hypocrites of Madinah {trap}swore by Allah that they were part of the believers.{/trap} The verse says they were not. Ibn Kathir explains they {trap}stayed with the believers unwillingly{/trap}, out of fear and necessity, not from affection.
now: You stay in the circle, the group, even the marriage, but only because leaving would cost you. You say the right words at gatherings. {idea}Ask what keeps you there: fear, or real love for Allah and for these people?{/idea}
old: Showing up and saying I belong is enough.
new: Belonging means my heart is there too, not just my fear.
try: Do one thing for your community this week that no one requires of you.

title: Any cave or hole, and they would bolt to it.
subtitle: Looking for the nearest exit
then: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah explained it: if they found {trap}a fort, a mountain cave, or a tunnel in the ground{/trap}, they would rush into it to get away from the believers. They were among them in body, {trap}always looking for the exit.{/trap}
now: During the khutbah you check the time. In the Quran class you plan your excuse to leave early. {idea}When your heart keeps hunting for the exit from good things{/idea}, that is worth noticing and gently treating.
old: Leaving early from good things is harmless.
new: A heart always looking for exits from good is a heart that needs care.
try: Stay until the very end of the next khutbah or class without checking your phone.

title: Pleased when given, angry when not.
subtitle: Fairness judged by my own share
then: Some accused the Prophet ﷺ of being unfair in dividing the charity. Ibn Kathir mentions a man who, after Hunayn, told him: be fair. He ﷺ replied that he would be lost if he were not. Ibn Kathir notes {trap}they did not object for the religion's sake, but to get more for themselves.{/trap}
now: The bonus split at work. The inheritance. Who got the bigger room. {trap}Your sense of justice is loudest when your own share is small.{/trap} {idea}Ask whether you would object just as hard if you had been given more.{/idea}
old: I complain because it is unfair, not because of my share.
new: My idea of fair can quietly bend around what I receive.
try: Think of one thing you feel was unfair to you. Ask if you would care if it favored you.

title: If only they had said: Allah is enough for us.
subtitle: Contentment, trust, and hope
then: After the complaints about the charity, the verse shows the better way: {idea}being content with what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ gave{/idea}, saying {idea}Allah is sufficient for us{/idea}, and {reward}Allah will give us of His bounty.{/reward} Ibn Kathir calls it a gracious kind of conduct with an honorable secret.
now: You did not get the raise, the house, the rishta you hoped for. Your chest tightens. {idea}Try these words instead of the complaint{/idea}: hasbuna Allah, Allah will give us from His bounty. Hope pointed at Him, not at people.
old: When I get less, I have every right to be bitter.
new: Allah is enough for me, and He has more bounty than anyone.
try: When you feel shortchanged today, say: hasbunallah, sayu'tinallahu min fadlih.

title: Allah Himself named who the zakah is for.
subtitle: Eight doors of care
then: After the hypocrites accused the Prophet ﷺ of unfair division, Allah {idea}named the recipients Himself.{/idea} The Prophet ﷺ described the truly needy as {reward}the one who does not have enough, whose need is not noticed, and who does not ask people.{/reward} Safwan bin Umayyah said the gifts he received turned hatred into love.
now: The neighbor who never complains but whose fridge is nearly empty. The student far from home whose card got declined. {idea}The verse widens your eyes{/idea}: the people zakah is meant for are often the quiet ones right near you.
old: The needy are the people who ask.
new: Often the most in need are the ones who never ask.
try: Think of one quiet person near you who might be struggling. Help them discreetly.

title: They mocked him as all ears. He is an ear of good.
subtitle: Mistaking kindness for gullibility
then: Some hypocrites hurt the Prophet ﷺ by saying {trap}he is all ears: if we swear to him, he will believe us.{/trap} The reply: {idea}he is an ear of good for you{/idea}, believing in Allah, trusting the believers, and {reward}a mercy to those who believe.{/reward} Ibn Kathir adds he knew who spoke truth and who lied.
now: You give people the benefit of the doubt and someone calls you naive. You listen patiently to the colleague who goes on and on. {reward}Being a good listener is a strength and a mercy{/reward}, not a sign that you are easy to fool.
old: If I listen kindly to everyone, people will take advantage.
new: Listening well is a mercy, and it can go with a clear mind.
try: Give one person your full attention today, phone away, until they finish speaking.

title: They swear to please you. Allah is more worthy of pleasing.
subtitle: Whose approval are you chasing
then: Qatadah reports that a hypocrite spoke scornfully of the Prophet's message; a Muslim heard and reported it. Summoned, the man {trap}swore by Allah he never said it{/trap}, while the Muslim prayed: O Allah, confirm the truthful and expose the liar. This verse came: {idea}Allah and His Messenger ﷺ are more worthy to be pleased.{/idea}
now: You get caught saying something unkind and your instinct is to deny it, to smooth it over, to win back their approval. {idea}It would be better to own it before Allah{/idea}, and then make it right with them honestly.
old: As long as people are satisfied with my answer, I am fine.
new: Allah's pleasure matters more than smoothing things over with people.
try: Admit one small thing you said or did wrong, simply, without excuses.

title: Do they not know where opposing Allah leads?
subtitle: Choosing a side against Allah

row.title: I can drift and be fine
do I know where this leads?

then: Following the false oath, the verse asks: {idea}do they not know?{/idea} Ibn Kathir explains opposing Allah as {trap}standing on one side while Allah and His Messenger ﷺ are on the other.{/trap} That, the verse says, is {trap}the great disgrace.{/trap}
now: Small, steady choices put you somewhere: the jokes you join, the deals you make, the people you defend. {idea}Every so often, check which side your choices are adding up to{/idea}, and step back to Allah's side while the door is open.
old: I am not against Allah, I am just doing my own thing.
new: My choices, added up, place me on a side. I want it to be Allah's.
try: Look at one habit and ask: does this put me closer to Allah or further away?

title: Afraid a surah would come down and expose their hearts.
subtitle: The surah called the Exposer
then: Mujahid said the hypocrites would talk among themselves, then add: {trap}we hope Allah does not expose this secret of ours.{/trap} Qatadah said this is why the surah was also called {idea}Al-Fadihah, the Exposer{/idea}, because it laid bare what the hypocrites concealed.
now: The thing you said in the private chat, the thought you would never want shown on a screen. {idea}Allah already knows it.{/idea} That is not a threat to fear but a reason to clean the inside, so nothing there needs hiding.
old: What I say in private stays private.
new: Allah knows my hidden words. Let my private self be one I am not ashamed of.
try: Delete one private message or thread you would be ashamed for Allah to see. Ask His forgiveness.

title: We were only joking. About Allah and His verses?
subtitle: Some things are not material for jokes

row.title: Allah, His verses, His Messenger ﷺ?

then: Ibn Umar said that during Tabuk a man mocked the Quran reciters as {trap}hungry, lying and cowardly.{/trap} When it reached the Prophet ﷺ, the man clung to the Prophet's camel saying {trap}we were only chatting and joking.{/trap} The Prophet ﷺ recited: {idea}was it Allah, His verses and His Messenger you were mocking?{/idea}
now: The meme about the beard, the hijab, the angels. The group laughs and you laugh along. Or the joke is yours. {idea}"Just a joke" does not change what was laughed at.{/idea} Some things are too precious to be punchlines.
old: It was only a joke. No one meant anything by it.
new: Mocking Allah, His verses or His Messenger ﷺ is serious, even as a joke.
try: The next time a joke touches the sacred, do not laugh, and gently change the subject.

title: Some jokes are not just jokes.
subtitle: When the excuse comes after the mockery
then: During the campaign of Tabuk, a man in a gathering mocked the Quran reciters as greedy, lying, and cowardly. When it reached the Prophet ﷺ, the man ran to him saying {trap}we were only talking idly and joking.{/trap} The reply was this verse: {idea}make no excuse.{/idea}
now: The group chat where someone posts a meme mocking the prayer, or the people who keep it. You add a laughing emoji because everyone else did. Later, if asked, you would say it was only a joke. {idea}The verse says the laugh itself was a choice.{/idea}
old: If I was joking, it does not really count.
new: Mocking what is sacred counts, whatever tone I used.
try: Next time a joke about faith comes up, simply do not join it. Silence is enough.

title: They forgot Allah, so He left them forgotten.
subtitle: The habits that make up hypocrisy
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the hypocrites were the mirror image of the believers. They {trap}encouraged evil, discouraged good, and closed their hands{/trap} from spending in Allah's cause. They forgot the remembrance of Allah, and so He treated them {trap}as if He had forgotten them.{/trap}
now: A colleague suggests padding the expense report and you nod along. A friend wants to volunteer and you say it is a waste of a Saturday. Your phone gets your morning; Allah gets whatever is left. {idea}Forgetting rarely feels like a decision. It just happens one day at a time.{/idea}
old: Forgetting Allah for a while is harmless. He will still be there.
new: The way I treat Allah's remembrance is the way I am treated.
try: Put one short remembrance of Allah on the first thing you do tomorrow morning.

title: Where the pattern of hypocrisy finally leads.
subtitle: A promise, spoken plainly

key.label: Why it is called a promise

row.title: a promise kept
sub: Allah does not break His word

then: Right after listing the habits of hypocrisy, the verse names where they lead. Ibn Kathir says this is {trap}on account of their evildoing{/trap} just described. The curse, he explains, means being {trap}expelled from Allah's mercy.{/trap}
now: You read a warning like this and quietly assume it is about someone else. But the verse before was about habits: urging wrong, blocking good, holding back. Those are things anyone can slide into. {idea}A warning is a mercy when it arrives early enough to change course.{/idea}
old: Warnings like this are for other people, not for me.
new: The warning is about habits, and habits can still be changed today.
try: Pick one habit from the verse before. Ask Allah sincerely to keep it far from you.

title: Stronger and richer people walked this road before.
subtitle: Enjoying your share and losing the point
then: The hypocrites were compared to nations before them who had more strength, wealth, and children. They enjoyed their portion and {trap}indulged in lies and falsehood{/trap}, and their deeds came to nothing. The Prophet ﷺ warned that people would follow those before them {trap}hand span by hand span.{/trap}
now: You scroll through people who have more: the bigger house, the louder life. You copy the habits along with the look. Nobody decides to follow; it just happens one trend at a time. {idea}The verse asks you to notice whose footsteps you are in.{/idea}
old: I am just living like everyone else around me.
new: Following the crowd step by step can lead me where they ended.
try: Notice one habit you picked up only because everyone does it. Drop it for a day.

title: Allah wronged no one; they wronged themselves.
subtitle: The news of past nations as a lesson

row.title: self-wrong
sub: they saw proof and turned away

then: Ibn Kathir explains this as advice to the hypocrites: have you not learned the end of nations who rejected their messengers? Each was given {idea}clear proofs and unequivocal evidence.{/idea} So when the end came, {trap}it was not Allah who wronged them.{/trap}
now: Your doctor shows you the test results twice. Your friend warns you about the debt, kindly, more than once. When it finally catches up with you, it is tempting to call it bad luck. {idea}Often the warning was clear. The choice was yours.{/idea}
old: Bad things just happened to those people.
new: They were warned clearly, and the harm came from their own turning away.
try: Think of one clear warning you keep ignoring, in health, money, or faith. Act on it once.

title: Believers hold each other up like one building.
subtitle: The opposite picture to the hypocrites
then: After the traits of the hypocrites, Allah describes the believers. They {idea}help and aid each other.{/idea} The Prophet ﷺ said the believer to the believer is {idea}like a building, its parts supporting each other{/idea}, and crossed his fingers together.
now: A friend in your circle loses her job. One person sends a message, another quietly shares a lead, a third reminds everyone to pray for her. Nobody is a hero; everyone is a brick. {reward}That is what the verse calls allies.{/reward}
old: My faith is my own private matter.
new: My faith is meant to hold others up, and theirs to hold me.
try: Message one believing friend today just to ask how they are really doing.

title: Gardens are promised, but His pleasure is greater.
subtitle: The highest gift above the gift
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah's pleasure is {reward}grander and better{/reward} than all the delights of Paradise. He cites the Prophet ﷺ: Allah will ask the people of Paradise if they are pleased, then grant them His pleasure and {reward}never be angry with them afterwards.{/reward}
now: You finish a hard project and your manager says the bonus is coming. Then they add, I am genuinely proud of you. Somehow the second line is what you remember on the drive home. {idea}Being accepted matters more than being paid.{/idea}
old: Paradise is mostly about the rewards I will get.
new: The greatest reward is that Allah is pleased with me.
try: Do one good deed today hoping only that Allah is pleased, and tell no one.

title: Firm with those who plot, merciful with believers.
subtitle: A command to the Prophet, and its limits
then: Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to strive hard against open enemies and the hypocrites, and also {reward}to be merciful with the believers.{/reward} Ibn Abbas said the striving against hypocrites was {idea}with the tongue{/idea}, by ending the lenient treatment that let their plotting continue.
now: The striving left to you starts closer than any battlefield. It is the voice in you that wants to skip the prayer, fake the excuse, or say one thing and mean another. {idea}Be firm with that voice.{/idea} Then be soft with your family, your neighbor, the people praying beside you.
old: Strictness is for other people who are doing wrong.
new: The first hypocrisy I am asked to be stern with is my own.
try: Name one excuse you often give yourself. Today, do not accept it.

title: They swore they never said it, and they had.
subtitle: A door to repentance left open
then: Al-Julas said that if the Prophet ﷺ was truthful, they were worse than donkeys. His stepson Umayr, who loved him, reported it. Al-Julas {trap}swore by Allah he never said it.{/trap} The verse exposed him, yet said {reward}if they repent, it is better for them.{/reward} It is reported he repented sincerely.
now: You said something unkind about a friend in another chat, and now they have heard. The easiest move is to deny it, or swear it was taken out of context. {idea}The verse shows a harder, better door: own it and turn back.{/idea}
old: Once I am caught, denying is the only way to save myself.
new: Even after being exposed, turning back is still better for me.
try: If you owe someone an admission, say the simple truth to them today.

title: If He gives me more, I will give.
subtitle: The promise made while waiting for wealth
then: Ibn Kathir says some hypocrites gave Allah their {trap}strongest oaths{/trap} that if He enriched them, they would give alms and be among the righteous. He adds that {idea}Allah knows the secret and what is more hidden{/idea}, even the pretended intention to give.
now: When the promotion comes, I will start giving monthly. When the business takes off, I will help my parents properly. The future version of you is always generous. {idea}The verse looks at the present version.{/idea}
old: I will be generous once I can afford it.
new: The giver I promise to become later is shaped by what I give now.
try: Give a small amount today, sized to what you have now, not what you hope for.

title: The money came, and the promise went.
subtitle: When bounty arrives, stinginess shows
then: This continues the story from the verse before. Ibn Kathir notes that when Allah gave them of His bounty, {trap}they did not fulfill their vows{/trap} or say the truth with their words. They {trap}turned away, averse{/trap}, as if the promise had never been made.
now: Payday arrives and the charity link you saved last month sits unopened. The raise you prayed for comes, and somehow the bills grow to match. {idea}Nothing dramatic. Just a slow turning away from what you said you would do.{/idea}
old: I meant my promise; things just got more expensive.
new: What I do when the blessing arrives shows what my promise really was.
try: Recall one promise you made to Allah when you were in need. Keep a piece of it today.

title: Broken promises leave hypocrisy behind in the heart.
subtitle: How a habit becomes a condition
then: Ibn Kathir says hypocrisy was placed in their hearts {trap}because they broke their promise and lied.{/trap} He cites the Prophet ﷺ: the signs of a hypocrite are three, {idea}when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, when trusted he betrays.{/idea} He adds: we seek refuge with Allah from such an end.
now: I will call you back. I will be there by six. I will pay you Friday. Small promises, broken so often they stop feeling like promises at all. {idea}The verse shows that small habits can settle into who you are.{/idea}
old: Small broken promises are just part of busy life.
new: Each kept promise guards my heart from becoming what I fear.
try: Keep one small promise today exactly as you said it, even if it costs you.

title: He knows the secret, and what is quieter still.
subtitle: No private conversation is private from Him
then: This closes the story of those who promised charity and then held back. Ibn Kathir says Allah knows {idea}the secret and what is more hidden than the secret{/idea}, even when they pretended they would give. {idea}Allah knows them better than they know themselves.{/idea}
now: The side conversation in a private chat. The message you typed and deleted. The reason you gave your boss versus the reason you actually skipped the meeting. {idea}All of it is open to Allah.{/idea} That can feel heavy, or it can feel like relief: someone sees the whole truth of you.
old: What I say in private stays private.
new: Nothing is hidden from Allah, so I can stop performing.
try: Before one private conversation today, ask yourself if you would say it the same way in front of Allah.

title: They mocked the big giver and the small giver.
subtitle: The man who brought a handful of dates

row.title: Abu Aqil
sub: a Sa of dates, a night's work

row.title: the effort
sub: all both of them had to give

then: When the Prophet ﷺ called for charity, Abdur-Rahman bin Awf gave thousands and was called a show-off. Abu Aqil worked all night drawing water, earned two measures of dates, and brought one. They laughed: {trap}Allah does not need this.{/trap} The verse defended {reward}both givers{/reward}, and Ibn Kathir notes the recompense is like the deed.
now: Someone posts that they donated and the comments say attention seeker. Someone gives five dollars at the mosque and a person behind them smirks. {trap}Mockers always find an angle.{/trap} The verse says Allah saw the night of work behind the small coins.
old: My small gift is too little to matter.
new: Allah weighs my effort, not the size next to someone else's.
try: Give something small today without apology, and never comment on anyone else's giving.

title: Even seventy prayers for them would not be enough.
subtitle: The Prophet's mercy, and a closed door

row.title: the Prophet ﷺ
sub: ready to ask again and again

then: Ibn Kathir explains that seventy is how Arabs {idea}speak of no limit{/idea}, to close the subject. When Abdullah bin Ubayy died, the Prophet ﷺ still went to his funeral at his son's request, saying {reward}I will ask seventy times and seventy more.{/reward} His mercy was that wide.
now: You may lean on your mother's prayers, the friend who always makes dua for you, the good family you came from. Those are gifts. But no one else can turn your heart for you. {idea}The door opens from your side.{/idea}
old: My family's prayers will carry me even if I drift.
new: Others can pray for me, but turning to Allah is mine to do.
try: Ask Allah's forgiveness yourself today, in your own words, for one specific thing.

title: Do not go out in the heat, they said.
subtitle: Escaping one discomfort into a greater one
then: Tabuk came at a time of {trap}intense heat{/trap}, when fruit was ripe and shade was sweet. Those who stayed behind rejoiced and told each other: {trap}do not march in the heat.{/trap} The reply: the Fire is more intense. Ibn Kathir says if they had understanding, they would have gone.
now: The alarm for Fajr goes off and the bed is warm. A friend needs help moving on the hottest Saturday of the year. You tell yourself it is not the right moment. {idea}The verse asks which discomfort you are really running from, and toward.{/idea}
old: I will do the hard good thing when it is more comfortable.
new: Running from small discomfort can lead to a far greater one.
try: Do one good thing today that you have been delaying only because it is uncomfortable.

title: Laugh a little now, weep much later.
subtitle: Short laughter, long consequence
then: Those who stayed behind from Tabuk were pleased with themselves. Ibn Abbas commented: {idea}life is short, so let them laugh as they like in it.{/idea} When they return to Allah, {trap}the crying begins.{/trap} The verse ties it to what they used to earn.
now: You dodged the shift, skipped the duty, and laughed with friends about how clever it was. The laugh felt good for an evening. {idea}The verse asks you to think past the evening{/idea}, to the account where every choice is earned.
old: Getting out of something is a small win worth laughing about.
new: The laugh is short; what I earned by it stays.
try: Think of one duty you escaped recently. Make it up to someone today.

title: You chose to sit once, so sit now.
subtitle: One choice shaping the next
then: The Prophet ﷺ was told that if those who stayed behind later asked to join, the answer was no: {trap}you were pleased to sit the first time.{/trap} Ibn Kathir draws a lesson: {idea}an evil deed is often followed by another, and a good deed by another good deed.{/idea}
now: You skip the gym once, then it is easier to skip twice. You pray on time today, and tomorrow it is a little more natural. Choices are not isolated; they lay down tracks. {idea}Whatever you choose now makes the next choice easier.{/idea}
old: One missed chance does not affect the next one.
new: Each choice makes the next one like it easier.
try: Do one good deed today, then follow it right away with a second small one.

title: The Prophet ﷺ stood at a funeral, and Allah answered.
subtitle: The funeral of Abdullah bin Ubayy

row.title: the son
sub: asks for the shirt, the prayer

then: When Abdullah bin Ubayy, the chief of the hypocrites, died, his son asked the Prophet ﷺ for his shirt as a shroud and to pray over him. {reward}The Prophet ﷺ gave both.{/reward} Umar objected, then said he was amazed at his own daring. {idea}Soon after, this verse came.{/idea}
now: You may know someone whose life seemed full of opposition to faith, and now they are gone. The verse shows the Prophet's ﷺ mercy went very far, and that final judgment belongs to Allah alone. {idea}Your part is your own state when your time comes.{/idea}
old: I need to decide where others ended up.
new: Judgment is Allah's; my concern is how I will die.
try: Ask Allah today, in your own words, to let you die in a state He loves.

title: Do not be dazzled by their wealth and children.
subtitle: When blessings turn into a burden
then: This repeats an earlier verse of the same surah, as Ibn Kathir notes briefly. The setting is the same: the hypocrites around Madinah had {reward}wealth and sons{/reward}, and it would be easy to admire them. The verse says those very things {trap}could become their punishment.{/trap}
now: The cousin with the big wedding photos. The colleague whose kids are in every highlight reel. You feel small next to them. {idea}The verse says what you see on the outside tells you nothing about what it costs inside.{/idea}
old: People with more must be more blessed than me.
new: Having more is not proof of being loved more by Allah.
try: When you feel envy today, say Alhamdulillah for one specific thing you have.

title: Those with the most means asked to stay home.
subtitle: Having the ability and asking to be excused
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah rebuked those who stayed back {trap}even though they had the supplies, means and ability.{/trap} They said: leave us with those who sit. He adds that such people are boastful when it is safe and {trap}fearful when it is hard.{/trap}
now: You have the car, the free evening, the skills. Your elderly neighbor needs a lift to the clinic, and you find a reason to say no. {idea}The verse is not about those who cannot. It is about those who can and do not.{/idea}
old: I am excused because I am busy too.
new: When I have the means, my excuse needs to be honest.
try: Use one thing you have plenty of today, time, a car, a skill, to help someone.

title: Content to stay behind, until the heart stopped understanding.
subtitle: How comfort can seal a heart
then: Continuing the verse before, they were {trap}content to be with those who sit behind.{/trap} Ibn Kathir says their hearts were sealed because they stayed away, so they no longer understood {trap}what benefits them or what hurts them.{/trap}
now: At first, skipping the circle or the Quran class feels like a break. A month later you do not even miss it. A year later the reminders sound like noise. {idea}The verse warns that contentment with less can quietly dull your sense of what matters.{/idea}
old: I am just taking a break from the good things for a while.
new: Being content to stay behind can slowly dull my heart.
try: Reconnect with one good habit you dropped. Do just five minutes of it today.

title: But the Messenger and the believers gave what they had.
subtitle: The contrast to those who stayed home
then: After describing the faults of the hypocrites, Ibn Kathir says Allah {idea}praised the faithful believers{/idea} who strove with the Prophet ﷺ in the heat of Tabuk. For them are {reward}the good things{/reward} in the Hereafter.
now: The call might be small: a sick relative, a fundraising night, a friend who needs you at the hospital at midnight. Some people find reasons; some people just show up. {idea}The verse calls the ones who show up successful.{/idea}
old: Showing up costs me too much.
new: Giving what I have when called is what success looks like.
try: Say yes today to one request for help you would normally decline.

title: What was prepared for those who went.
subtitle: Gardens already waiting
then: This completes the verse before. Ibn Kathir says these two verses describe {idea}the qualities and the reward{/idea} of the faithful believers. Those who left the shade of Madinah for the heat find gardens {reward}prepared for them{/reward}, the high grades of Paradise.
now: You give up the lie-in for Fajr, the weekend for your parents, the extra money for someone in need. It feels like loss at the time. {reward}The verse says something has already been prepared in return.{/reward}
old: What I give up for Allah is simply gone.
new: What I give up is answered with something already prepared for me.
try: Give up one small comfort today for Allah's sake, and tell no one.

title: Some came with excuses; some did not even ask.
subtitle: Two kinds of staying behind
then: Ibn Kathir describes bedouins living around Madinah who came to the Prophet ﷺ {idea}to explain their weakness and inability{/idea} to join. Ibn Abbas said they had valid excuses. Others, who {trap}had lied to Allah and His Messenger{/trap}, simply stayed home without asking.
now: You cannot make it to your friend's event. One way is to call, explain honestly, and apologize. The other is to go quiet, leave the messages on read, and hope no one notices. {idea}The verse treats those two very differently.{/idea}
old: If I cannot do it anyway, explaining does not matter.
new: How honestly I face what I cannot do matters to Allah.
try: If you are avoiding someone because you let them down, send an honest message today.

title: No blame on the weak, the sick, or the poor.
subtitle: When a real excuse holds you back
then: Ibn Kathir lists real excuses: lasting weakness, temporary illness, or poverty. There is no sin, he says, {idea}provided they do not spread malice or discourage others{/idea} while they remain behind. The Prophet ﷺ said some who stayed in Madinah {reward}were with you{/reward} in every valley, held back only by their excuse.
now: You are in a hospital bed while your family does the Ramadan charity drive. Or money is tight and you cannot give this year. {reward}A sincere heart that cannot go still travels with them.{/reward} What matters is that you cheer them on instead of tearing them down.
old: If I cannot take part, I am left out of the reward.
new: When I am truly unable, sincerity carries me alongside those who go.
try: If something holds you back today, make dua for the people who are doing it.

title: They walked away in tears because they could not go.
subtitle: The ones who had no mount
then: Some came to the Prophet ﷺ asking for mounts so they could join. He said {trap}I can find nothing for you to ride.{/trap} They turned back with {reward}eyes overflowing with tears{/reward}. Mujahid said it was revealed about Bani Muqarrin from Muzaynah.
now: You wanted to go for Umrah with your parents this year and the money is not there. You watch the photos come in from others and your eyes sting. {reward}That sting is not nothing. Allah sees it and honors it.{/reward}
old: Wanting to do good but being unable is just a disappointment.
new: Sincere longing for a good I cannot reach is itself seen by Allah.
try: Tell Allah today about one good thing you long to do but cannot yet. Ask Him for it.

title: The blame falls on the rich who asked out.
subtitle: Means without will
then: Right after the poor who wept, the verse turns to those {trap}who were rich and still asked to stay behind.{/trap} Ibn Kathir says Allah sealed their hearts, so they {trap}know not what they are losing.{/trap}
now: The two verses sit side by side for a reason: a poor man crying because he cannot give, and a rich one relieved because he does not have to. You may be richer in some things than you think: time, health, a free weekend. {idea}Ask which side of the contrast you are on.{/idea}
old: If I can get out of it, I have not lost anything.
new: Turning down good when I have the means is a loss I may not even feel.
try: Name one blessing you have plenty of. Use part of it for someone else today.

title: Excuses lined up for the return home.
subtitle: Your deeds will be seen, then shown to you
then: When the believers returned to Madinah, Ibn Kathir says the hypocrites {trap}began apologizing.{/trap} The answer: Allah has told us your news. {idea}Allah and His Messenger will see your deeds{/idea}, and then you return to the Knower of the seen and unseen, who will inform you of what you did.
now: You missed the deadline and you are drafting the perfect email: traffic, a sick kid, a broken laptop. Some of it is even true. {idea}The verse says the words matter less than what you do from here.{/idea}
old: If I explain it well enough, it will be fine.
new: Better deeds from here count more than a better excuse.
try: Next time you owe an apology, keep it short and then show the change instead.

title: They swore so you would leave them alone.
subtitle: An oath used to avoid being questioned
then: Ibn Kathir says the hypocrites swore to the believers {trap}so they would be left without admonishment.{/trap} Allah ordered the believers to turn away from them, for their inner state was impure, and their end {trap}a recompense for what they used to earn.{/trap}
now: Oh I swear, wallahi, it was not me. Sometimes the oath is not about truth; it is about ending the conversation before anyone asks more. {idea}The verse notices that move, and asks you to notice it in yourself.{/idea}
old: Swearing by Allah settles the matter.
new: Using Allah's name to dodge questions makes the wrong heavier, not lighter.
try: Go one full day without swearing by Allah to make anyone believe you.

title: People may be satisfied with you; Allah may not.
subtitle: Whose approval actually counts

key.label: Who you are really answering to
