then: The hypocrites swore {trap}so that the believers would be pleased with them.{/trap} Ibn Kathir explains: even if the believers forgave them, {idea}Allah is not pleased{/idea} with those who rebel against His obedience. Fisq, he adds, means deviation.
now: Your manager accepts your explanation. Your parents stop asking. Your friends say no worries. Everyone is fine with you, and you feel relieved. {idea}The verse asks a quieter question: is Allah pleased?{/idea}
old: Once people are satisfied, the issue is closed.
new: Being cleared by people is not the same as being right with Allah.
try: Before one decision today, ask: would this please Allah, not just the people around me?

title: Distance from knowledge can harden a heart.
subtitle: Why being far from learning matters
then: Ibn Kathir notes there were {idea}disbelievers, hypocrites and believers{/idea} among the desert Arabs, as the next verses show. Living far from the Prophet ﷺ, they were {trap}more likely not to know{/trap} what had been revealed. He cites the hadith: {trap}whoever lives in the desert becomes hard-hearted.{/trap}
now: You moved for work, far from your old masjid and the friends who reminded you. No class, no circle, just podcasts you rarely open. {idea}You do not feel worse. You just know a little less every year.{/idea} The verse names what distance from learning can do to anyone.
old: I can stay close to Allah without staying close to learning.
new: Staying far from knowledge slowly hardens any heart, including mine.
try: Learn one new thing about your faith today from a trusted teacher or book.

title: Giving felt like a fine, so they hoped for disaster.
subtitle: When spending feels like a loss
then: Ibn Kathir says some of them saw what they spent {trap}as a loss and a burden{/trap}, and waited for afflictions to strike the believers. The verse says evil would touch them instead. {idea}Allah hears and knows{/idea} who deserves what.
now: The zakah calculation comes out higher than you hoped, and you feel robbed. A friend's business struggles and a small part of you is glad. {trap}Resentment about giving and quiet hope that others fall can grow together.{/trap}
old: Every bit I give is money lost.
new: If giving feels like a fine, my heart needs attention, not my wallet.
try: Give a small amount today and say, this is for my nearness to Allah.

title: Others from the same desert gave to come near.
subtitle: Same place, opposite hearts
then: Ibn Kathir calls these {reward}the praiseworthy bedouins.{/reward} They gave charity seeking nearness to Allah and the Messenger's prayers for them. The verse confirms: {reward}it is a means of nearness for them{/reward}, and Allah will admit them to His mercy.
now: Two coworkers get the same bonus. One complains about the tax. The other quietly sends part of it to a family in need and asks them to pray for her. {idea}Same office, same paycheck, opposite hearts.{/idea}
old: My surroundings decide what kind of person I become.
new: In any surroundings, I can make giving a way to come near to Allah.
try: When you give today, ask the person to make dua for you.

title: Allah is pleased with them, and they with Him.
subtitle: The first ones, and those who follow well

row.title: mutual pleasure
sub: He with them, they with Him

then: After many verses on those who stayed behind, the surah turns to {reward}the foremost{/reward}: the Muhajirin and Ansar. Scholars Ibn Kathir cites said they were those who gave the pledge at Hudaybiyyah, or who prayed toward both qiblahs. Then come {idea}those who followed them with excellence.{/idea}
now: You may feel your faith is second-hand, learned from an app, a parent, a convert friend's story. The verse leaves a place in the circle for {idea}those who followed well{/idea}, long after the first ones. Being late does not lock you out.
old: The great reward was only for the first generation.
new: Following their lead with excellence brings me into the same pleasure.
try: Read about one of the early Companions today and copy one small habit of theirs.

title: You do not know them; We know them.
subtitle: Hypocrisy no one could see, not even the Prophet ﷺ

row.title: know myself
sub: the only file I can read

then: Ibn Kathir says the Prophet ﷺ {idea}used to see them day and night{/idea} without knowing exactly who they were. Qatadah drew a lesson: some people claim to know who is in Paradise and who is in the Fire, yet {trap}do not know their own end.{/trap} You know more about yourself than about anyone else.
now: Someone in the comments says that scholar is a hypocrite, that cousin is going to Hell, that family is not real Muslims. It sounds confident. {idea}The verse says even the Prophet ﷺ was not given that knowledge of everyone.{/idea} Your own heart is the only one you can check.
old: I can usually tell who is sincere and who is fake.
new: Only Allah knows hearts; my job is to examine my own.
try: The next time you want to judge someone's faith, look at your own instead.

title: They admitted it: good deeds mixed with a bad one.
subtitle: Hope for people who are partly good
then: Ibn Kathir says these were believers who stayed away from Tabuk {idea}out of laziness and preferring comfort{/idea}, not doubt. Abu Lubabah and some friends tied themselves to the masjid pillars until the Prophet ﷺ would untie them. When this verse came, {reward}he untied and pardoned them.{/reward} The verse covers all who mix good and bad.
now: You pray, you are kind to your parents, you give. And there is one thing you keep doing that you are not proud of. {reward}The verse is for you.{/reward} Not hiding it, not excusing it, just admitting it to Allah is where the door opens.
old: My bad deed cancels out the good in me.
new: Admitting the bad alongside the good is the start of being forgiven.
try: Tell Allah plainly about one wrong you keep repeating. Ask Him to turn to you.

title: Charity cleans the giver, and a prayer comforts them.
subtitle: What giving does for the one who gives
then: Allah told the Prophet ﷺ to take charity {reward}to purify and sanctify{/reward} the givers, and to pray for them. Whenever charity was brought, he would pray for the family who brought it, like {reward}O Allah, bless the family of Abu Awfa.{/reward} Ibn Abbas said his prayer was a mercy for them.
now: You transfer your zakah and close the app. It feels like a bill paid. But giving is also a wash for you: the attachment loosens, the heart lightens. {idea}And when someone thanks you and prays for you, that prayer is a gift back.{/idea}
old: Charity is something I lose for someone else's benefit.
new: Charity cleans and comforts me as much as it helps them.
try: When someone gives to you or helps you today, make a short dua for them out loud.

title: Your charity reaches Allah's Hand first.
subtitle: He accepts both repentance and giving

row.title: raised and grown
sub: like a pony raised with care

then: Ibn Kathir says this verse {idea}encourages repentance and charity{/idea}, each of which erases sins. The Prophet ﷺ said Allah receives charity in His Right Hand and {reward}raises it as one of you raises a young horse, until a bite becomes like Uhud.{/reward} Ibn Masud said charity reaches Allah's Hand before the needy's hand.
now: The few coins in the masjid box. The meal you bought the man outside the station. The small transfer you almost did not bother with. {reward}It does not stay small.{/reward} Allah takes it and raises it, the way you raise something you love.
old: What I can afford to give is too small to matter.
new: Allah accepts even a little and grows it far beyond what I gave.
try: Give something small today, a meal, a few coins, and pair it with a quiet repentance.

title: Do your deeds; they will be seen.
subtitle: Seen by Allah, His Messenger, and the believers
then: Mujahid saw this as a warning to those who defy Allah: their deeds will be shown. Aishah said: if someone's good deeds please you, recite this verse. The Prophet ﷺ said {idea}do not be pleased with anyone's deeds until you see how they end{/idea}, for people change in both directions.
now: You are on a good streak: praying on time, reading every day. Or you are in a bad one and feel it is too late. {idea}Neither is the end of your story.{/idea} The verse simply says: keep working, it is all seen.
old: My current streak, good or bad, defines me.
new: What I keep doing to the end is what will be shown.
try: Do one good deed today as if it might be the last thing on your record.

title: Three men left waiting for Allah's decision.
subtitle: When your case is still open
then: Ibn Abbas and others said these were {idea}three Companions{/idea} who stayed behind from Tabuk out of laziness, not doubt. Unlike Abu Lubabah's group, they did not tie themselves up, and their pardon {trap}was delayed.{/trap} Ibn Kathir adds: they were at Allah's mercy, and {reward}His mercy comes before His anger.{/reward}
now: You repented, you meant it, and still the guilt has not lifted. No sign, no relief yet. {reward}Waiting is not the same as rejection.{/reward} These three men waited too, and the answer came later in this very surah.
old: If I do not feel forgiven yet, I am not.
new: Waiting for Allah's answer can still end in His mercy.
try: Keep up one sincere act of repentance today even if you do not feel any change yet.

title: A mosque built to harm and divide.
subtitle: When something good-looking is built for bad

picture.label: What they said and what it was

then: A man named Abu Amir turned against the Prophet ﷺ and sought outside help to fight him. He told some hypocrites in Madinah to build a base. They built a mosque {trap}next to the masjid of Quba{/trap} and asked the Prophet ﷺ to pray in it, saying it was for the weak on rainy nights. {idea}Allah testified they were lying.{/idea}
now: A new group in the community, with a nice name and a good cause, but every meeting ends with talk against the other masjid. A project you start partly to outshine someone. {idea}The verse asks what you are really building, and why.{/idea}
old: If it looks religious, the intention must be good.
new: Something can look like worship and still be built to divide.
try: Look at one thing you are involved in. Ask honestly: does it bring people together?

title: A mosque founded on taqwa from the first day.
subtitle: Quba, and people who love to be clean
then: Ibn Kathir says Quba was built {idea}from the first day on taqwa{/idea}, to gather the believers. The Prophet ﷺ said {reward}one prayer in Quba is like an Umrah{/reward}, and he used to visit it riding and walking. He asked its people about their purification, which Allah had praised.
now: Maybe it is a small, old prayer room with worn carpets, where the same quiet people come every Fajr and take care with their wudu. Nothing about it trends online. {idea}That is often what a place founded on taqwa looks like.{/idea}
old: The impressive places are where real worship happens.
new: A place built on taqwa, with people who keep themselves clean, is what Allah loves.
try: Make your next wudu slowly and carefully, as someone Allah loves for purifying.

title: Built on taqwa, or on the edge of a crumbling bank.
subtitle: What your life is resting on
then: Ibn Kathir explains that a masjid built on {idea}taqwa and Allah's pleasure{/idea} is not the same as one built to harm and divide. The second was built {trap}on the edge of a steep hole{/trap} that gives way. Jabir said he saw smoke rising from the harmful mosque in the Prophet's ﷺ time.
now: A career built on cutting corners. A friendship built on gossip about others. A marriage built on keeping up appearances. They can stand for years. {trap}Then one day the ground under them gives way.{/trap} The verse asks what you are building on.
old: If it is standing, it must be built well.
new: What lasts is what rests on taqwa, not what looks solid now.
try: Pick one thing you are building, a habit, a plan, a relationship. Check its foundation.

title: What they built kept doubt alive inside them.
subtitle: How a wrong project stays in the heart
then: Ibn Kathir says that because of this awful act, {trap}they inherited hypocrisy in their hearts{/trap}, the way calf worshippers stayed attached to the calf. Many early scholars said {trap}until their hearts are cut{/trap} means until they die. {idea}Allah knows and is wise{/idea} in repaying every deed.
now: Maybe you once helped start a rumor about someone. It is long over, everyone has moved on. But you still feel uneasy around that person, still defensive when it comes up. {idea}What we build against others can keep living in us.{/idea} Turning back sooner is a mercy.
old: Once it is over and done, it no longer affects me.
new: A wrong I built can stay in my heart until I sincerely undo it.
try: Undo one old wrong quietly today: a kind word, an apology, a correction.

title: Allah bought what He already gave you, and paid Paradise.
subtitle: The sale every believer carries

row.title: Allah
sub: who gave them in the first place

key.label: What it says about your worth

row.title: He raised the price
sub: bought you and raised your worth

then: In the setting of Tabuk, Allah describes a sale: the believers' lives and wealth for Paradise. Ibn Kathir calls it {reward}His favor and generosity{/reward}, since He accepts as payment what He already owns. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: {reward}Allah bought them and raised their worth.{/reward}
now: Shimr bin Atiyyah said every Muslim has a sale on their neck, to fulfill or leave unfinished. Yours might be the hours you give your sick mother, the salary you share, the energy you spend on what Allah loves. {idea}Every bit of it is part of the deal.{/idea}
old: What I give up for Allah leaves me poorer.
new: Allah takes what He gave me and pays me Paradise for it.
try: Choose one thing you will spend today purely for Allah: an hour, a sum, an effort.

title: Who the buyers are: nine plain qualities.
subtitle: The people of the sale described
then: Ibn Kathir says this is {idea}the description of the believers{/idea} from whom Allah bought their souls and wealth. They repent, worship, praise, and fast, which he says is the meaning of {idea}as-sa'ihun{/idea} here. They pray, guide others to good, and keep Allah's limits, so they worship their Lord and advise His creation.
now: You read a list like this and feel far from it. Look at the first word: {idea}those who repent.{/idea} Not those who never fall. The list starts where you are when you turn back, and grows from there.
old: These qualities belong to people far better than me.
new: The list starts with turning back, which I can do today.
try: Pick one quality from the list and practice it once today, starting with a repentance.

title: Even love for family has a limit set by Allah.
subtitle: The Prophet's ﷺ grief for his uncle and his mother
then: When his uncle Abu Talib was dying, the Prophet ﷺ begged him: {reward}O uncle, say La ilaha illallah{/reward}, and I will plead for you. Abu Talib chose his fathers' religion. Visiting his own mother's grave, the Prophet ﷺ was {trap}more tearful than they had ever seen him.{/trap} Allah said: you do not guide whom you love.
now: Your brother has drifted far. Your father mocks your prayer. You love them and it hurts. {idea}Even the Prophet ﷺ could not make the heart of the one he loved most turn.{/idea} Keep loving, keep praying for them while they live, and leave the heart to Allah.
old: If I love them enough, I can bring them to faith.
new: I can love, invite, and pray, but guidance belongs to Allah.
try: Make a sincere dua today for one relative who is far from faith, while they are alive.

title: Ibrahim kept a promise to his father, then let go.
subtitle: A tender heart and a clear line
then: When the Prophet ﷺ mentioned that Ibrahim had prayed for his father, this verse explained it: {idea}it was a promise he had made.{/idea} Ibn Abbas said Ibrahim kept praying for him until he died, then dissociated. Ibn Masud said awwah means {reward}one who calls on Allah constantly.{/reward}
now: You made a promise to someone you love, and you keep it as long as you honestly can. When a line has to be drawn, you draw it without hardness. {idea}Ibrahim shows that tenderness and firmness can live in the same heart.{/idea}
old: Drawing a line with family means I stopped caring.
new: I can keep my promises, accept Allah's limits, and stay gentle.
try: Turn to Allah in a short private dua today, like Ibrahim the awwah, about someone you love.

title: Allah makes clear what to avoid before He holds you to it.
subtitle: Guidance comes before accountability
then: Ibn Abbas said some believers used to pray for relatives who died opposing Allah, until the verses before came. Ibn Jarir explained: {reward}before He informs you an action is not allowed{/reward}, you have not disobeyed Him. Mujahid said it is also a general call: {idea}beware of disobeying Him and be eager to obey.{/idea}
now: You learn something new about your faith and feel a wave of panic about all the years you did not know. The verse is a calm hand on your shoulder. {reward}Allah is just.{/reward} What matters is what you do now that you know.
old: I am guilty for everything I did before I knew better.
new: Allah makes things clear first; what I do after knowing is what counts.
try: Act on one thing you learned recently, without dwelling on the years before.

title: He owns the heavens and earth, gives life and death.
subtitle: No protector or helper besides Him
then: After the verses about praying for relatives, this verse turns the believers back to Allah alone. Ibn Jarir said it is {idea}a command to trust in Allah's aid{/idea}, for He owns the heavens and earth, and {reward}not to fear His enemies.{/reward}
now: Your visa is stuck, the job offer depends on one person's signature, a test result is due Thursday. You keep refreshing your inbox as if someone there holds your fate. {idea}Everything in that inbox belongs to Allah too.{/idea}
old: My future depends on the people who control my situation.
new: Allah owns every situation and is the only true protector.
try: When you check on something you are anxious about today, say first: Allah is enough for me.

title: Forgiven in the hour of hardship.
subtitle: When even faithful hearts almost wavered
then: Tabuk came in a year of {trap}little rain, intense heat, and scarce water.{/trap} Qatadah said two men would share one date. Umar recalled thirst so hard they thought their necks would break, until the Prophet ﷺ raised his hands and {reward}rain fell on their camp.{/reward} Ibn Jarir said some hearts nearly doubted from the hardship.
now: A long illness, a year of rejections, a stretch where your prayers feel like they hit the ceiling. Somewhere in there a quiet voice asks if any of this is real. {reward}The verse says Allah saw that hour, and forgave, and held them steady.{/reward}
old: If my faith shook during hard times, it was never real.
new: Allah knows how hard the hour is and turns to the hearts that nearly slipped.
try: In your next hard moment, say: O Allah, keep my heart firm.

title: The earth closed in on them, and only He was refuge.
subtitle: Kab bin Malik and fifty nights

row.title: "Be happy, Kab!"
sub: the best day of his life

then: Kab said he was never wealthier than the year he stayed behind. He kept delaying, telling himself {trap}I can do that if I want{/trap}, until the army had gone. Over eighty men gave excuses; he told the Prophet ﷺ the truth. After fifty nights of silence, a voice cried from a mountain: {reward}Kab, be happy!{/reward}
now: You missed the moment by putting it off one day at a time. Now the room has gone cold, people avoid your eyes, and your own house feels strange. {idea}Kab did not run to the outside offer or a better story.{/idea} He waited on Allah, and the relief came.
old: When everyone turns away, I need a way out on my own.
new: When everything closes in, the only real refuge is Allah Himself.
try: If something heavy is pressing on you, take it to Allah in a long sujood tonight.

title: Fear Allah, and be with the truthful.
subtitle: The lesson of Kab's honesty

key.label: What Kab called his greatest blessing

then: After his repentance was accepted, Kab said Allah saved him {idea}for telling the truth{/idea}, and vowed to speak only the truth for life. Ibn Kathir quotes the Prophet ﷺ: {reward}truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise.{/reward} A person keeps striving for truth until written as truthful.
now: Your boss asks why the report is late. Your mother asks where you were. A small lie would be so smooth. {idea}Kab had the words for the perfect excuse too.{/idea} The verse asks you to stand with the truthful, even when it costs.
old: A small lie is easier on everyone.
new: The truth, even when it costs, is what saves me.
try: Tell the plain truth today in one moment where a small lie would be easier.

title: Every thirst, every tired step, is written down.
subtitle: No effort for Allah is wasted
then: Ibn Kathir says those around Madinah who stayed back from Tabuk {trap}preferred to preserve themselves{/trap} over sharing the Prophet's ﷺ hardship. They lost the reward written for those who went: every thirst, every fatigue, every hunger, even things {reward}not under their control{/reward}, recorded as good deeds.
now: The night shift where you stayed patient. The tired walk to the masjid in the rain. The hunger of a long fast at work. You think none of it counts because nothing big came of it. {reward}Allah does not let the reward of those who do good be lost.{/reward}
old: The hard parts of doing good are just the price, not the reward.
new: Every bit of tiredness for Allah's sake is written as a good deed.
try: When you feel tired doing something good today, quietly intend it for Allah.

title: Small or large, every coin and valley is written.
subtitle: Uthman's camels and the ordinary traveler

row.title: by the best
sub: of what they used to do

then: When the Prophet ﷺ urged spending on the army of hardship for Tabuk, Uthman bin Affan pledged {reward}a hundred camels, then a hundred more, then a hundred more.{/reward} The verse also counts the {idea}small contribution{/idea}. Qatadah said: the farther people go from their families for Allah, the nearer they are to Him.
now: You are not Uthman. Your gift is ten dollars and a Saturday morning driving boxes to the food bank. {reward}Small or large, the verse says it is written.{/reward} And Allah repays by the best thing you did, not the average.
old: Only big sacrifices really count with Allah.
new: Every small or large effort is written, and repaid by my best.
try: Give something small today for a good cause and trust that it is recorded.

title: Not everyone goes out; some must stay and learn.
subtitle: A community that keeps its knowledge

picture.label: How the community divided its work

then: Ibn Abbas said the believers should not all leave the Prophet ﷺ alone. While some went out, others stayed {idea}and learned what was revealed{/idea}, then taught the returning group: Allah revealed this to your Prophet, and we learned it. The verse speaks of gaining {idea}understanding in the religion{/idea} and warning one's people.
now: In your family or circle, maybe no one has really studied the faith. Everyone is busy with work and kids, and questions go to random videos. {idea}The verse says someone needs to be the one who learns, then comes back and shares.{/idea} It could be you.
old: Learning the faith deeply is for scholars, not for people like me.
new: My circle needs someone who learns and brings it back.
try: Learn one thing about your faith properly today, and share it with one person.

title: Allah is with those who have taqwa.
subtitle: A battlefield command and how it ends
then: This command was given to the believers in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, as part of the Tabuk era. Ibn Kathir explains the firmness as {trap}in battle{/trap}, and says the complete believer is {reward}kind to his believing brother.{/reward} He reads the closing words as: trust in Allah, knowing {idea}He is with you if you fear and obey Him.{/idea}
now: Your life is not a battlefield. What carries over is how the verse ends: success rests on {idea}taqwa{/idea}, not on how tough you look. At home, at work, in the family chat, the believer is known first for softness with those close to them.
old: Being strong and tough is what wins.
new: Allah's company comes with taqwa, and that is what truly wins.
try: Be extra gentle today with one family member you are usually short with.

title: Which of you did this surah increase in faith?
subtitle: The same verses, two very different effects
then: Some hypocrites asked each other mockingly, after a surah came down, {trap}which of you has had his faith increased by it?{/trap} Allah answered that the believers {reward}did grow in faith, and rejoiced.{/reward} Ibn Kathir calls this one of the strongest proofs that faith increases and decreases.
now: You sit in a Friday khutbah. The person next to you scrolls. You hear one line that lands, and your chest feels lighter for the rest of the day. {reward}Same words, same room.{/reward} The verse says what you bring to the Quran shapes what it does to you.
old: My faith is just at whatever level it is.
new: Each verse I take in with an open heart can raise my faith.
try: Read a few verses today slowly, and ask Allah to increase your faith through them.

title: The same medicine makes a sick heart sicker.
subtitle: When guidance meets a diseased heart
then: Ibn Kathir says the surah only {trap}adds doubt and suspicion{/trap} to what those with sick hearts already had. He gives a picture: {trap}someone upset by a certain food{/trap} gets more upset when fed more of it. Yet the Quran is {reward}a healing{/reward} for those who believe.
now: Every reminder irritates you lately. The khutbah feels preachy, the friend's post feels judgmental, the verse feels aimed at you. {idea}Before blaming the reminder, check the heart that is receiving it.{/idea}
old: If a reminder annoys me, the reminder must be the problem.
new: If guidance irritates me, my heart may need healing.
try: Next time a reminder annoys you, pause and ask Allah to soften your heart toward it.

title: Tested once or twice a year, and still no turning.
subtitle: Missing the lesson in hardship
then: Mujahid said they were tested {trap}with drought and hunger.{/trap} Ibn Kathir explains that they neither repented from their past sins {trap}nor learned a lesson for the future.{/trap} The trials came again and again, and nothing changed.
now: Every winter the same scare: a lump, a layoff rumor, a car crash that almost happened. You promise to change, then the fear fades and the promise fades with it. {idea}The verse asks you to let the next trial actually change something.{/idea}
old: Hard times are just something to survive and forget.
new: Each trial is a chance to repent and remember before the next one.
try: Recall your last real scare. Do one thing today you promised to do back then.

title: Does anyone see you? Then they slipped away.
subtitle: Turning from the truth, and being turned
then: When a surah was revealed, the hypocrites would look right and left, {trap}does anyone see you?{/trap}, then slip away. Ibn Kathir says they do not stay where truth is being declared. He links it to another verse: {trap}when they turned away, Allah turned their hearts away.{/trap}
now: The talk at the masjid starts, and you glance at the door, check your phone, slip out during the pause. No one notices. {idea}The verse notices.{/idea} Each small exit makes the next one easier, until staying feels impossible.
old: Leaving early does not matter if no one sees.
new: Each time I turn from the truth, my heart turns a little further.
try: Stay until the end of the next reminder or talk you attend, even if you want to leave.

title: Your hardship weighs on him; he is eager for you.
subtitle: The Messenger's ﷺ care for his people
then: After a long surah of warnings, it closes with mercy. Ibn Kathir notes this verse is among {idea}the last revealed{/idea}. The Prophet ﷺ said: {reward}I am holding you by the waist so you do not fall into the Fire, like moths.{/reward} He also said this religion is easy.
now: You may picture the faith as a list of things you get wrong. This verse shows a face full of concern for you. Every struggle you have, the debt, the anxiety, the habit you cannot break, {reward}would have grieved him ﷺ.{/reward} He wanted ease for you.
old: The Prophet ﷺ feels distant, a source of rules.
new: The Prophet ﷺ is grieved by my hardship and eager for my good.
try: Send salawat on the Prophet ﷺ ten times today, thinking of his care for you.

title: If they turn away, Allah is enough for me.
subtitle: The last words of the surah

row.title: their acceptance
sub: if they agree, I am okay

then: The surah ends with the Prophet ﷺ told what to say if people turn away from what he brought: {idea}Allah is sufficient for me.{/idea} Ibn Kathir says the Throne is above all creation, and {reward}everything is under His power{/reward}. Zayd bin Thabit said he found this final verse with Khuzaymah bin Thabit.
now: You did your best: the gentle advice, the patience, the invitation. And they still walked away, unfollowed you, stopped calling. {idea}You do not have to carry that alone.{/idea} Hasbiyallah. The One who holds the Throne is enough.
old: If people reject me, I have failed and I am alone.
new: When people turn away, Allah is still enough for me.
try: When someone turns away from you today, say: Hasbiyallahu la ilaha illa Huwa, alayhi tawakkaltu.
